title: La impresora de la sala 2
label: ch:es-oficina
canDo: I can deal with a workplace machine that is not working: read a notice saying a printer is out of service, say what I want to print and what I cannot connect, and offer to make or return a phone call.

payoff.summary: Read a notice taped to a printer and a message from a colleague, then say what you will do.
payoff.note: THE SIBLING CHECK CAUGHT THREE DEFECTS THAT THE PLAN HAD NOT. Run as `ls ES-C4NN-*.md` plus opening every non-zero grep hit ascending, it produced: (1) ES-C432-lavadora ALREADY OWNS -dora FOR MACHINES, with the exact secadora/calculadora table the impresora draft had duplicated, so impresora cites it and teaches the thing lavadora cannot -- that imprimir yields BOTH a person and a machine (el impresor / la impresora), which makes the article carry the meaning. Lavar has no human washer in ordinary speech, so -dora was free there; printing was a trade first. (2) THE DRAFT CONTRADICTED ITS OWN PREREQUISITE: it explained el ordenador's masculine gender as a dropped Spanish noun, but ES-C393-ordenador teaches that the computing sense came from FRENCH ordinateur. The ordenador row was removed rather than patched. (3) ES-C431-pedido's participle-noun table ALREADY PRINTS `| llamar | la llamada |`, and ES-C439-cortar already uses se ha cortado la llamada. So la llamada is cited and handed over, not introduced -- the same move imprimir makes with el impreso. UNTAUGHT WORDS CAUGHT BEFORE COMMIT. A first draft of conectar built a Grammar Lens contrasting conectar / encender / enchufar; a word-boundary grep returned only the draft file itself for all three of encender, enchufe and enchufar, so they are untaught across the whole corpus and were being presented as known. The lens was rebuilt on conectar vs conectarse, which is real, useful and made of taught material. Same class of defect in imprimir: `pulse el boton verde` uses pulsar, which the corpus does not teach (ES-C388-empujar mentions only Latin pulsare and English pulse), and it is an usted imperative besides. Replaced with `voy a imprimir el documento`. Also dropped: el cable, la red and quedarse sin tinta, none taught. AN ATOM ID WAS INVENTED. The conectar draft required ES-LEX-C393-TECH-01, which exists nowhere in the corpus; ES-C393-ordenador introduces ES-LEX-ORDENADOR. Corrected, and the prerequisite moved to ES-C393-internet so that internet is genuinely reviewed by conectarse a internet rather than named in passing -- ordenador stays in the closure as internet's own prerequisite. CONECTAR IS NOT AN INHERITED WORD. The Academy's dictionary derives it from English to connect, itself built on Latin conectere (con- plus nectere, to tie). The draft had said the word sat in Spanish waiting for wires; the truth is better, because chapter 393 already gave the learner two other routes -- ordenador, an old Spanish word that borrowed a MEANING from French, and internet, an English word borrowed whole. Conectar is the third route: an English word borrowed as a SHAPE, carrying Latin parts back to a Latin language. The repaso makes that three-way the chapter's point. roots are [connect-english, nectere-latin]. ETYMOLOGY OWNERSHIP RESPECTED. ES-C03-llamar (sequence 140) owns clamare AND the cl- to ll- sound law, with exclaim, proclaim, acclaim and clamor, so llamada cites it and adds only what it did not say: a llamada is still literally a crying-out, which is why una llamada de atencion is a warning and not a phone call. roots: [clamare], the bare slug ES-C03-llamar holds, so the two are cousins. imprimir and impresora take impressus-latin, the slug ES-C406-impreso holds, keeping verb and participle joined. THE GRAMMAR LENS IN LLAMADA IS DELIBERATELY HALF A RULE. ES-C49-participio owns -ado/-ido, so that is cited rather than claimed. What is new is the honest negative: the vowel is predictable and the ARTICLE is not. El pedido is masculine, la llamada and la entrada feminine, and nothing in pedir, llamar or entrar says which. Stated as a fact to learn with the word rather than papered over with a rule that does not hold. ES-C49-participios-irregulares does NOT list impreso, so imprimir adding it to hecho/dicho/visto/puesto, and to the later cubierto and roto, is new and is cited to that lesson. PRE-EXISTING DEFECT LOGGED, NOT FIXED HERE: ES-C432-lavadora's wrap-up asks where the -dor ending was first met and answers 'on the supplier' (ES-C431-proveedor, sequence 10470). ES-C297-tenedor at sequence 3990 teaches -dor as 'the ending that names whoever or whatever does the thing', with comedor and mirador. Proveedor is the second teaching, not the first. A THIRD DUPLICATION CAUGHT ON THE SIBLING PASS: ES-C432-contador ALREADY OWNS the rule that the -dor ending does not decide the article -- "this one is masculine where the washing machine was feminine, and nothing about the ending decides that". The impresora draft was re-teaching it as new. It now cites contador as settled and narrows its own claim to the thing contador cannot make: with lavadora and contador the article is a fact to memorise, whereas imprimir yields BOTH a person and a machine, so here the article is a CHOICE that carries the meaning. The la maquina impresora account is kept as the mechanism underneath contador's rule rather than as a competing one. The repaso was reworded the same way. CHECKED AND CLEAR: ES-C432-sintesis-aviso is also built round an AVISO, but it is a building notice to neighbours about water and meters, so the only overlap is the word aviso itself, which ES-C332-aviso teaches. No duplication.
